metric_rationale: The metric is the difference in TTB-consistent choice rates between non-tied conditions where tallying supports the TTB winner and conditions where tallying opposes it. TTB assigns the same binary score advantage to its winner in both sets, so it predicts a contrast near zero regardless of beta and epsilon; this within-subject subtraction also removes much of the variability caused by individual response-noise parameters. Tallying predicts a large positive contrast because its evidence points toward the TTB winner in the first set and away from that winner in the second. Pooling the three supporting and four opposing base conditions, including their reversals and repetitions, yields many observations per side and therefore a relatively stable subject-level estimate. Exact tally ties are excluded because they carry no directional tally prediction.

This metric measures behavioral alignment with the option favored by the highest-validity cue that discriminates. It is not merely an overall A/B response rate: exact stimulus reversals balance response side, so only a stimulus-contingent first-cue preference raises the score. Tallying is indifferent on every designed pair because each option wins equally many cues, predicting a match rate of 0.50. Take The Best predicts a rate above 0.50, potentially close to one depending on beta and epsilon. Averaging the diagnostic match indicator over all 96 trials gives a low-variance per-subject estimate and works identically on individual-subject and pooled data.

This is the final-reason capture rate: the fraction of trials on which the response follows the least-valid (latest encountered) discriminating cue. In every designed pair, that cue favors the option that loses the overall feature tally. Recency-Gated Reason Overwrite therefore predicts a capture rate above 0.5, attenuated by fatigue and lapses, whereas Tallying predicts a rate below 0.5 because it favors the feature-majority option. Exact A/B reversals ensure the contrast is not confounded with response side. Averaging all 96 trials gives a stable subject-level estimate while retaining a direct, interpretable test of which conflicting information controls choice.

This is the centered terminal-cue alignment effect. It equals +1 for choices following the lowest-validity/finally processed cue and -1 for choices opposing it. Tallying is indifferent on every presented pair, so it predicts an expectation of zero. Recency-Gated Reason Overwrite predicts a substantially positive value because the fourth cue usually overwrites the provisional decision. Unlike a raw A-choice rate, the signed contrast balances A- and B-favoring trials and therefore cancels stable response-side biases. It also averages all 96 binary observations per subject, giving relatively low between-subject sampling variance and high power for detecting the predicted gap.

This is the within-subject permutation effect on choosing the option supported by the final two cues. It subtracts terminal-option choice in AAAAABBBBB-type block trials from terminal-option choice in BBBAAAAABB-type mixed trials, pooling each trial with its exact A/B reversal. The advocated overwrite theory predicts a contrast near zero because both permutations have the same number of updates and the same two-cue terminal suffix. The retrospective-sampling theory predicts a large positive contrast: validity-biased retrieval disfavors the terminal option when it owns only the five weakest cues, but favors it when it owns the three strongest cues as well as the final two. Each component uses 48 repeated trials per subject, and the mirrored versions balance response-side tendencies, yielding substantially lower between-subject noise than a raw choice rate.

This is the proportion of long-conflict trials on which the subject chooses the option supported by the initial, high-validity cue run. It pools the 7- and 8-cue conditions and canonicalizes the A/B reversals, yielding 48 observations per subject and therefore relatively low sampling variance. Retrospective sampling predicts a high value because overload suppresses temporal recency and validity-biased accessibility favors the early 0.99/0.95 cues. Overwrite predicts a much lower value because the terminal run continues to determine the retained choice; fatigue only contracts that terminal preference toward chance. Restricting the metric to the long conditions avoids adding short-condition choice noise where both theories make similar terminal-choice predictions.

This metric tests the qualitative segmentation signature on the 8- and 10-reason trials, where the competing theory's quadratic switch interference is strongest. It first recodes choices as agreement with the terminal cue, making exact A/B reversals contribute identically, and contrasts terminal-following rates for low-switch versus switch-dense sequences. Recency-gated overwrite predicts almost no contrast because both patterns end in two cues favoring the same option; any prefix effect must survive two near-certain overwrites. Directional-run chunking predicts a substantial low-switch advantage because switch-dense sequences approach chance while coherent terminal chunks retain control. Thresholding at an 8-percentage-point practically meaningful effect yields a bounded, interpretable diagnostic expected to be 0 under overwrite and 1 under chunking, while its per-subject variance can never exceed 0.25.

Terminal displayed-cue agreement pools all 96 trials into a low-variance, side-balanced diagnostic. Directional-run chunking predicts that the terminal displayed run controls choice, so this proportion should be well above 0.5. Overwrite scans by descending validity instead; its final attended cues are Experts 2 and 1, which favor the option opposite the terminal displayed cue on every designed pair, so it predicts a value well below 0.5. Exact A/B reversals prevent a generic response-side preference from creating the contrast.

This is first-reason choice alignment: +1 when the selected option is favored by the first discriminating expert and -1 otherwise. The balanced reversal schedule makes response-side biases and control by the shared final reason cancel. Under recency-gated overwrite, ABA and BBA have nearly identical final-reason-driven choice rates, as do their reversals, so positive alignment on first/last-concordant trials is canceled by negative alignment on first/last-discordant trials, yielding a value near zero. The competitive buffer preserves the first trace, producing systematically greater support for A in ABA than BBA and the symmetric effect in their reversals; all 96 trials contribute to a positive score, keeping within-subject sampling variance relatively low.

This metric measures choice agreement with the common two-cue suffix while weighting trials by prefix coherence. It gives greatest precision weight to the fully coherent condition, where the competitive-buffer theory predicts near-ceiling agreement, and progressively less weight to conditions whose surviving prefix traces oppose the suffix. The larger penalty for a conflict at the second cue reflects its stronger surviving buffer trace. Thus the statistic captures both the buffer theory's high overall suffix-consistent responding and its graded coherence profile. The overwrite theory instead predicts an almost flat profile because two terminal updates nearly eliminate prefix dependence; its count-based fatigue and larger lapse range also lower terminal agreement across all four conditions. Orienting reversals by the terminal cue removes response-side bias, and pooling all conditions gives a stable per-subject estimate from 96 trials.

The metric is the terminal-cue choice rate specifically in the 5- and 6-reason conditions, pooling 48 repeated trials per subject. These are the conditions with the sharpest theoretical disagreement: recency-gated overwrite predicts that the lowest-validity terminal reason usually controls choice, whereas dual-code arbitration predicts that the strong four-of-five or five-of-six global coalition overrides it. Coding choices relative to the terminal cue also combines the exact A/B reversals, canceling stable response-side bias. Pooling both diagnostic loads supplies many observations per subject and should keep between-subject measurement variance low without relying on the less-discriminating short and overloaded conditions.

This measures how often subjects choose the three-cue majority option specifically in the strongest coalition and averages the two exact A/B orientations equally. In these trials, the majority is supported by the 99%, 95%, and 90% experts, whereas the minority is supported only by the 56% and 51% experts. Dual-code arbitration predicts frequent majority choices because the strong validity-weighted global coalition can overturn the terminal minority-favoring local commitment. Overwrite predicts the opposite: the common A,A,A,B,B direction sequence leaves the terminal minority reasons in control and does not use the large validity gap. Restricting the score to the strongest coalition maximizes the predicted separation, while 32 repeated observations per subject and side balancing keep its between-subject sampling variance relatively small.
